summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed a law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence, carrying two to five years' imprisonment and fines. The law was passed unanimously by the military junta that has held power since September 2022. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that the penalty range of two to five years' imprisonment, together with fines, applies to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices".

The criminal prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code (CPF) approved by the junta's council in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law. Homosexuality had never before been outlawed in Burkina Faso; the ban took effect as criminal-code law on 1 September 2025.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has stated that foreigners will be deported under the law. A trans visitor therefore faces not only imprisonment and fines but removal from the country under a statute whose drafting and application in relation to trans people are not further specified in the available reporting.

The law was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. It was passed by a transitional legislature rather than an elected parliament, and the sources provide no indication of judicial review, complaint mechanism or other institutional recourse available to a person charged under it.
tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso joins roughly 22 of the 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations, placing it within a substantial regional pattern of criminalisation rather than outside it.

The prohibition did not arrive as a standalone statute on sexual conduct. It was folded into a broad rewrite of marriage and family law, so the Personal and Family Code is the operative instrument and the criminal penalty sits inside a wider package of family-law reform approved by the junta's council in July 2024.

Passage was unanimous in the transitional legislature, and the measure was announced by the presidency and defended publicly by the Justice Minister. The official framing presents the ban as deliberate government policy rather than an incidental consequence of the family-code revision.
localsOnly:
The statute applies to people present in Burkina Faso regardless of nationality, and the reported penalty range of two to five years' imprisonment plus fines is stated without any distinction between residents and visitors.

The same July 2024 overhaul of marriage and family law governs domestic family relations for Burkinabè residents, so the Personal and Family Code reaches the resident population's marriages, partnerships and household status as well as creating the criminal offence.

Residents live under a government that has ruled since September 2022 and that enacted the law amid a documented crackdown on opposition, media and civil space, conditions that bear on whether a person charged under the statute could mount a public defence or seek institutional protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement practice since the law took effect on 1 September 2025 is unresolved. The available sources report the passage, the penalties and the deportation provision, but no arrests, prosecutions, sentence lengths or documented police conduct under the new offence.

The reach of the phrase "homosexual or similar practices" as used by Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala is unresolved. Whether the provision captures gender identity, gender expression or trans people specifically is not stated in the sources, and no trans-specific case or guidance is sourced here.

The sources do not address whether Burkina Faso has any legal framework for recognition or change of gender markers on identity or travel documents, and no entry, visa or border-screening rule specific to trans travellers is sourced. The existing position on legal gender recognition before 1 September 2025 is likewise not sourced.

Whether the Transitional Legislative Assembly's proceedings, or any court, offered an avenue to challenge the law is not sourced beyond the fact of unanimous passage. Reported detail stops at the enactment date.
